claim: Granule cells of the cerebellum make up to 175,000 excitatory synapses on a single Purkinje cell.
source: Granule cells of the cerebellum make up to 175,000 excitatory synapses on a single Purkinje cell, encoding the wide variety of information from the mossy fibre inputs into the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a factual statement about cerebellar anatomy that is directly stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Napper and Harvey, 1988 elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: The granule cell axon is made of an ascending portion and a long parallel fibre extending at right angles.
source: The granule cell axon is made of an ascending portion and a long parallel fibre extending at right angles, an architecture suggesting that synapses formed by the two segments of the axon could encode different information.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about granule cell morphology, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: There are controversial indications that ascending axon (AA) and parallel fibre (PF) synapse properties and modalities of plasticity are different.
source: There are controversial indications that ascending axon (AA) and parallel fibre (PF) synapse properties and modalities of plasticity are different.
evidence: This statement references existing literature with conflicting findings, as evidenced by citations to studies by Isope and Barbour, 2002, Walter et al., 2009, and Sims and Hartell, 2005, 2006 in the introduction.

claim: Synchronous AA and PF repetitive train stimulation, with inhibition intact, triggers long-term potentiation (LTP) at AA synapses specifically.
source: We show for the first time that synchronous AA and PF repetitive train stimulation, with inhibition intact, triggers long-term potentiation (LTP) at AA synapses specifically.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The timing of the presentation of the two inputs controls the outcome of plasticity.
source: Furthermore, the timing of the presentation of the two inputs controls the outcome of plasticity and induction requires NMDAR and mGluR1 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 demonstrating different plasticity outcomes with different timing intervals.

claim: AA-LTP induction requires NMDAR activation.
source: Furthermore, the timing of the presentation of the two inputs controls the outcome of plasticity and induction requires NMDAR and mGluR1 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C showing that APV (NMDAR antagonist) blocks AA-LTP.

claim: AA-LTP induction requires mGluR1 activation.
source: Furthermore, the timing of the presentation of the two inputs controls the outcome of plasticity and induction requires NMDAR and mGluR1 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing that CPCCOEt (mGluR1 antagonist) blocks AA-LTP.

claim: In fish, discrimination of self from external stimuli has been shown to rely on associating motor command and sensory feedback in cerebellar-like structures.
source: In fish, discrimination of self from external stimuli has been shown to rely on associating motor command and sensory feedback in cerebellar-like structures (Montgomery and Bodznick, 1994; Sawtell, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Montgomery and Bodznick, 1994 and Sawtell, 2017.

claim: The cerebellum is involved in motor learning and coordination.
source: The role of the cerebellum in motor learning and coordination has been well documented, but it is now clear that it is also involved in a number of higher cognitive functions (Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998; Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998 and Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2010.

claim: The cerebellum is involved in higher cognitive functions.
source: The role of the cerebellum in motor learning and coordination has been well documented, but it is now clear that it is also involved in a number of higher cognitive functions (Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998; Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998 and Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2010.

claim: An AA can form multiple synapses with a few overlaying PCs in the same sagittal plane as the GC soma.
source: As a consequence, an AA can form multiple synapses with a few overlaying PCs in the same sagittal plane as the GC soma, distributing information to a restricted number of cells, whereas PFs course through the dendritic trees of hundreds of PCs along the lobule (Napper and Harvey, 1988), distributing information widely to other microzones.
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by citation to Napper and Harvey, 1988.

claim: PFs course through the dendritic trees of hundreds of PCs along the lobule.
source: As a consequence, an AA can form multiple synapses with a few overlaying PCs in the same sagittal plane as the GC soma, distributing information to a restricted number of cells, whereas PFs course through the dendritic trees of hundreds of PCs along the lobule (Napper and Harvey, 1988), distributing information widely to other microzones.
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by citation to Napper and Harvey, 1988.

claim: PC activity might be principally driven by local GCs via AA synapses.
source: This morphology and functional data have suggested that PC activity might be principally driven by local GCs via AA synapses (Cohen and Yarom, 1998), while distant GCs might modulate its activity via the PF system to provide the PC with less specific contextual information.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Cohen and Yarom, 1998.

claim: Distant GCs might modulate PC activity via the PF system to provide the PC with less specific contextual information.
source: This morphology and functional data have suggested that PC activity might be principally driven by local GCs via AA synapses (Cohen and Yarom, 1998), while distant GCs might modulate its activity via the PF system to provide the PC with less specific contextual information.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on anatomical and functional considerations.

claim: In the adult rat, an estimated 175 k excitatory PF synapses encode information on the dendritic tree of a single PC.
source: In the adult rat, an estimated 175 k excitatory PF synapses encode information on the dendritic tree of a single PC (Napper and Harvey, 1988).
evidence: This is a quantitative anatomical fact supported by citation to Napper and Harvey, 1988.

claim: Two PF synaptic populations with different molecular signatures have been identified.
source: We previously identified two PF synaptic populations with different molecular signatures (Devi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a prior finding by the authors supported by citation to Devi et al., 2016.

claim: 85% of PF synapses are silent.
source: Isope and Barbour, 2002 estimated that 85% of PF synapses are silent, as suggested by in vivo data (Ekerot and Jörntell, 2001), however, that proportion was significantly lower for local GCs and presumably AA synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Isope and Barbour, 2002 and Ekerot and Jörntell, 2001.

claim: The proportion of silent synapses is significantly lower for local GCs and presumably AA synapses.
source: Isope and Barbour, 2002 estimated that 85% of PF synapses are silent, as suggested by in vivo data (Ekerot and Jörntell, 2001), however, that proportion was significantly lower for local GCs and presumably AA synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Isope and Barbour, 2002.

claim: The properties of AA synapses were found to be indistinguishable from PF synapses in studies by Isope and Barbour, 2002 and Walter et al., 2009.
source: In this study and that by Walter (Walter et al., 2009), the properties of AA synapses were found to be indistinguishable from PF synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Isope and Barbour, 2002 and Walter et al., 2009.

claim: AA and PF synaptic properties and susceptibility to plasticity are different according to Sims and Hartell, 2005.
source: On the other hand, a study by Sims and Hartell, 2005, has shown that AA and PF synaptic properties and susceptibility to plasticity are different.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sims and Hartell, 2005.

claim: AA synapses were shown to be refractory to plasticity with well-described protocols.
source: AA synapses were shown to be refractory to plasticity with well-described protocols.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sims and Hartell, 2005 and 2006 in the following sentence.

claim: Neither associative CF-mediated long term depression (LTD) nor LTP could be induced at AA synapses.
source: Neither associative CF-mediated long term depression (LTD) nor LTP could be induced (Sims and Hartell, 2005; Sims and Hartell, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sims and Hartell, 2005 and Sims and Hartell, 2006.

claim: The amplitude of the AA-EPSC increased to 131 ± 7% of baseline 25–30 min after induction (n=24).
source: The amplitude of the AA-EPSC increased to 131 ± 7% (n=24) of baseline 25–30 min after induction (p=7e-5 one-tailed T-test, n=24).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 1B, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The PF-EPSC decreased to 65 ± 5% of baseline 25–30 min after induction (n=25).
source: The PF-EPSC on the other hand decreased slowly to 65 ± 5% (n=25) of baseline (p=1e-7 one-tailed T-test, n=25).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 1B, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The average amplitude of the AA-EPSC during baseline recordings was 110±12 pA (median 90 pA).
source: On average, the amplitude of the AA-EPSC during baseline recordings was 110±12 pA (median 90 pA) and PF-EPSC 480 ± 100 pA (median 288 pA, n=25), and the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) was PPRAA 1.93 ± 0.08 and PPRPF 1.89 ± 0.07.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from baseline recordings in the experiments.

claim: The average amplitude of the PF-EPSC during baseline recordings was 480 ± 100 pA (median 288 pA, n=25).
source: On average, the amplitude of the AA-EPSC during baseline recordings was 110±12 pA (median 90 pA) and PF-EPSC 480 ± 100 pA (median 288 pA, n=25), and the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) was PPRAA 1.93 ± 0.08 and PPRPF 1.89 ± 0.07.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from baseline recordings in the experiments.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio was PPRAA 1.93 ± 0.08 and PPRPF 1.89 ± 0.07.
source: On average, the amplitude of the AA-EPSC during baseline recordings was 110±12 pA (median 90 pA) and PF-EPSC 480 ± 100 pA (median 288 pA, n=25), and the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) was PPRAA 1.93 ± 0.08 and PPRPF 1.89 ± 0.07.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from baseline recordings in the experiments.

claim: The AA-EPSC was 80 ± 6% of baseline (n=16) 25–30 min after the Iclamp period in No Stim experiments.
source: On average, 25–30 min after the Iclamp period, the AA-EPSC was 80 ± 6% of baseline (n=16, significantly smaller than baseline p=0.0004, and significantly smaller than synchronous stimulation protocol p=10e-7)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PF-EPSC was 81 ± 8% of baseline (n=17) 25–30 min after the Iclamp period in No Stim experiments.
source: and the PF-EPSC was 81 ± 8% of baseline (n=17, not significantly smaller than baseline p=0.062, and not significantly larger than synchronous stimulation protocol p=0.106)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a rundown of the amplitude for both pathways during experimental time, independent of the induction protocol.
source: indicating a rundown of the amplitude for both pathways during experimental time, independent of the induction protocol.
evidence: This is inferred from the No Stim control experiments showing decreased amplitudes over time.

claim: The normalised PPRs are transiently decreased following induction, but return to their original value within 25–30 min.
source: As a result, the normalised PPRs are transiently decreased following induction, but return to their original value within 25–30 min (PPRAA 1.03 ± 0.03, PPRPF 0.99 ± 0.03, n=24, p=0.81).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 1B bottom panel.

claim: Changes in the PPR have been linked to a change in the presynaptic release probability.
source: Changes in the PPR have been linked to a change in the presynaptic release probability (Zucker and Regehr, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Zucker and Regehr, 2002.

claim: The transient decrease in PPR suggests a transient presynaptic effect on release probability following induction.
source: This suggests a transient presynaptic effect on release probability following induction and likely explains the progressive effects on AA and PF responses, but there was no significant long-term change in the PPR, suggesting that the long-term effects observed are linked to postsynaptic changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PPR data and established knowledge about PPR and release probability.

claim: The long-term effects observed are linked to postsynaptic changes.
source: This suggests a transient presynaptic effect on release probability following induction and likely explains the progressive effects on AA and PF responses, but there was no significant long-term change in the PPR, suggesting that the long-term effects observed are linked to postsynaptic changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of long-term PPR changes despite long-term amplitude changes.

claim: Stimulation of the AA pathway alone is not sufficient to trigger AA-LTP.
source: This shows that stimulation of the AA pathway alone is not sufficient to trigger AA-LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Stimulation of either pathway independently did not induce AA-LTP.
source: Stimulation of either pathway independently did not induce AA-LTP, showing that co-activation of AA and PF inputs is necessary, and AA-LTP is associative.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Co-activation of AA and PF inputs is necessary for AA-LTP.
source: Stimulation of either pathway independently did not induce AA-LTP, showing that co-activation of AA and PF inputs is necessary, and AA-LTP is associative.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: AA-LTP is associative.
source: Stimulation of either pathway independently did not induce AA-LTP, showing that co-activation of AA and PF inputs is necessary, and AA-LTP is associative.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments demonstrating the requirement for co-activation.

claim: When stimulating AAs 150 ms after PFs, the amplitude of the AA- and PF-EPSCs was depressed to a similar extent (AA was 53 ± 15% and PF 50 ± 20% of baseline, n=8).
source: Figure 2A shows that when stimulating AAs 150 ms after PFs, the amplitude of the AA- and PF-EPSCs was depressed to a similar extent (AA was 53 ± 15% and PF 50 ± 20% of baseline, n=8, not significantly different from each other p=0.84), transforming AA-LTP into LTD.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the timing experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Stimulating AAs 150 ms after PFs transforms AA-LTP into LTD.
source: Figure 2A shows that when stimulating AAs 150 ms after PFs, the amplitude of the AA- and PF-EPSCs was depressed to a similar extent (AA was 53 ± 15% and PF 50 ± 20% of baseline, n=8, not significantly different from each other p=0.84), transforming AA-LTP into LTD.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the timing experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When stimulating AAs 150 ms before PFs, the amplitude of the AA-EPSC was 97 ± 26% of baseline (n=7).
source: On the other hand, when stimulating AAs 150 ms before PFs (see Figure 2B), the amplitude of the AA-EPSC was first facilitated and declined back to baseline (AA after 25–30 min was 97 ± 26%, n=7, significantly smaller than synchronous stimulation p=0.011)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the timing experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When stimulating AAs 150 ms before PFs, the amplitude of the PF-EPSC was 84 ± 12% of baseline (n=7).
source: and the amplitude of the PF-EPSC was now close to baseline (84 ± 12%, n=7, not significantly larger than synchronous stimulation, p=0.062).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the timing experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The relative timing of the AA and PF input stimulation determines the extent of plasticity of both GC synapses.
source: These experiments show that the relative timing of the AA and PF input stimulation determines the extent of plasticity of both GC synapses, sometimes in opposite directions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the timing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: PF-LTD and LTP have been linked to mGluR1 activation.
source: PF-LTD and LTP have been linked to mGluR1 (Daniel et al., 1992; Konnerth et al., 1992; Hémart et al., 1995) and/or NMDAR activation (Casado et al., 2002; Bidoret et al., 2009; Bouvier et al., 2016; Kono et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Daniel et al., 1992; Konnerth et al., 1992; Hémart et al., 1995.

claim: PF-LTD and LTP have been linked to NMDAR activation.
source: PF-LTD and LTP have been linked to mGluR1 (Daniel et al., 1992; Konnerth et al., 1992; Hémart et al., 1995) and/or NMDAR activation (Casado et al., 2002; Bidoret et al., 2009; Bouvier et al., 2016; Kono et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Casado et al., 2002; Bidoret et al., 2009; Bouvier et al., 2016; Kono et al., 2019.

claim: KOs of either mGluR1 or NMDAR show defects in cerebellar learning.
source: and KOs of either receptor show defects in cerebellar learning (Aiba et al., 1994; Nakao et al., 2019; Kono et al., 2019; Schonewille et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aiba et al., 1994; Nakao et al., 2019; Kono et al., 2019; Schonewille et al., 2021.

claim: mGluR1s are highly expressed by PCs and located postsynaptically at GC to PC synapses.
source: mGluR1s are highly expressed by PCs and located postsynaptically at GC to PC synapses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the localization of mGluR1s in cerebellar circuits.

claim: mGluR1s activation requires PF train stimulation.
source: mGluR1s activation requires PF train stimulation, and it has not been observed when stimulating sparse GC synapses (Marcaggi and Attwell, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marcaggi and Attwell, 2005.

claim: NMDARs are expressed by molecular layer interneurons.
source: NMDARs on the other hand are expressed by molecular layer interneurons (Glitsch and Marty, 1999; Duguid and Smart, 2004) and GCs (Bidoret et al., 2009; Bidoret et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glitsch and Marty, 1999 and Duguid and Smart, 2004.

claim: NMDARs are expressed by GCs.
source: NMDARs on the other hand are expressed by molecular layer interneurons (Glitsch and Marty, 1999; Duguid and Smart, 2004) and GCs (Bidoret et al., 2009; Bidoret et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bidoret et al., 2009 and Bidoret et al., 2015.

claim: NMDARs are located on dendrites and presynaptic varicosities of GCs.
source: NMDARs on the other hand are expressed by molecular layer interneurons (Glitsch and Marty, 1999; Duguid and Smart, 2004) and GCs (Bidoret et al., 2009; Bidoret et al., 2015), where they are located on dendrites and presynaptic varicosities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bidoret et al., 2009 and Bidoret et al., 2015.

claim: NMDARs are not present postsynaptically at granule cell to Purkinje cell synapses.
source: NMDARs are not present postsynaptically at granule cell to Purkinje cell synapses (Llano et al., 1991; Piochon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Llano et al., 1991 and Piochon et al., 2007.

claim: mGluR1 receptor block impairs AA-LTP.
source: mGluR1 receptor block impairs AA-LTP. AA was 72 ± 13% of baseline (statistically smaller than control synchronous stimulation p=0.0004, n=7 and n=24, and the PF-EPSC wass 54 ± 8%, n=7, not significantly smaller than control synchronous stimulation, p=0.12, n=7)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments with CPCCOEt shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NMDAR activation is necessary for AA-LTP induction.
source: Both AA and PF pathways are depressed, showing that NMDAR activation is necessary for AA-LTP induction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from experiments with APV shown in Figure 3C.

claim: With NMDARs blocked, the AA- and PF-EPSCs were on average 50 ± 8% and 40 ± 9% of baseline 25–30 min after induction.
source: The AA- and PF-EPSCs were on average 50 ± 8% and 40 ± 9% of baseline 25–30 min after induction (n=6, significantly smaller than control p=2e-6, and n=7, p=0.027, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments with APV shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The concomitant involvement of both mGluR1s and NMDARs is required for the induction of plasticity at GC synapses.
source: These results show the concomitant involvement of both mGluR1s and NMDARs in the induction of plasticity at GC synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: GABAARs are present on GCs, including presynaptically on the GC axon.
source: GABAARs are also present on GCs, including presynaptically on the GC axon (Stell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stell et al., 2007.

claim: Presynaptic GABAARs are activated by the synaptic release of GABA and affect the axonal Cl- concentration and synaptic release.
source: These presynaptic GABAARs are activated by the synaptic release of GABA and affect the axonal Cl- concentration and synaptic release (Stell et al., 2007; Astorga et al., 2015; Berglund et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stell et al., 2007; Astorga et al., 2015; Berglund et al., 2016.

claim: PF-LTP in mice relies on GABAAR activation to hyperpolarize PC dendrites and allow the recruitment of T-type Ca2+ channels.
source: Binda et al., 2016 showed that PF-LTP in mice relies on GABAAR activation to hyperpolarize PC dendrites and allow the recruitment of T-type Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Binda et al., 2016.

claim: The recruitment of molecular layer interneuron-mediated inhibition can modify CF-mediated Ca2+ signals and LTD induction.
source: Rowan et al., 2018 also showed that the recruitment of molecular layer interneuron-mediated inhibition can modify CF-mediated Ca2+ signals and LTD induction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rowan et al., 2018.

claim: With GABAARs blocked, the AA-EPSC was 117 ± 24% of baseline after 25–30 min.
source: On average with GABAARs blocked, the AA-EPSC was initially facilitated after induction (170 ± 30%, n=9), but that potentiation decreased with time and it was 117 ± 24% of baseline after 25–30 min.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments with SR95531 shown in Figure 4.

claim: With GABAARs blocked, the PF-EPSC was 56 ± 10% of baseline at 25–30 min (n=9).
source: The decrease of the PF-EPSC at 25–30 min (56 ± 10%, n=9) was not significantly smaller than control values (p=0.19).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments with SR95531 shown in Figure 4.

claim: GABAAR activation seems to be required for efficient induction and maintenance of this type of associative plasticity.
source: GABAAR activation, therefore, seems to be required for efficient induction and maintenance of this type of associative plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments with SR95531 shown in Figure 4.

claim: When AA stimulation was replaced by sparse PF stimulation, the amplitude of the PF-sparse input was not increased as seen for AA inputs, but depressed.
source: When AA stimulation was replaced by sparse PF stimulation, the amplitude of the PF-sparse input was not increased as seen for AA inputs, but depressed.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both sparse and dense PF inputs are reduced on average to 88 ± 13% and 54 ± 10% of baseline after 25–30 min, respectively.
source: Both the sparse and dense inputs are reduced on average to 88 ± 13% of baseline (significantly smaller than control AA, p=0.0024, n=10 PF-sparse and n=24 AA control) and 54 ± 10% of baseline (significantly smaller than control PF, p=0.017, n=10 PF-dense and n=25 PF control) after 25–30 min, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sparse PF experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Associative LTP of the AA input is not due to the sparse distribution of stimulated AA synapses on PC dendrites, but to the stimulation of a population of synapses prone to a specific form of plasticity.
source: These experiments suggest that associative LTP of the AA input is not due to the sparse distribution of stimulated AA synapses on PC dendrites, but to the stimulation of a population of synapses prone to a specific form of plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the sparse PF experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The difference in plasticity observed between the AA and PF inputs is not linked to the distribution of synapses on the dendritic tree but to the different properties of the synapses.
source: We have shown that the difference in plasticity observed between the AA and PF inputs is not linked to the distribution of synapses on the dendritic tree but to the different properties of the synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the sparse PF experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The average length of a PF is between 4.2 and 4.7 mm.
source: The average length of a PF is between 4.2 and 4.7 mm (Pichitpornchai et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by citation to Pichitpornchai et al., 1994.

claim: Only granule cells located within the 50 µm thick layer of the PC dendritic tree can make AA synapses.
source: If we assume that only granule cells located within the 50 µm thick layer of the PC dendritic tree can make AA synapses, and take the average length of a parallel fibre, they represent only 1 to 2% of granule cells or parallel fibres.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical considerations and the average PF length.

claim: AA synapses represent only 1 to 2% of granule cells or parallel fibres.
source: If we assume that only granule cells located within the 50 µm thick layer of the PC dendritic tree can make AA synapses, and take the average length of a parallel fibre, they represent only 1 to 2% of granule cells or parallel fibres.
evidence: This is calculated based on anatomical considerations.

claim: Sims and Hartell (2005, 2006) reported the absence of both LTP and LTD at AA synapses associated with CF conjunctive stimulation.
source: To our knowledge, only Sims and Hartell (2005, 2006) examined plasticity at AA synapses and reported the absence of both LTP and LTD associated with CF conjunctive stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sims and Hartell, 2005 and 2006.

claim: Presynaptic GABAB and CB1 receptors have been shown to modulate the presynaptic release probability at granule cell to Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Presynaptic GABAB and CB1 receptors have been shown to modulate the presynaptic release probability at granule cell to Purkinje cell synapses, but they decrease release and increase the PPR (Dittman and Regehr, 1997; Safo and Regehr, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dittman and Regehr, 1997 and Safo and Regehr, 2005.

claim: Endocannabinoid release is triggered by mGluR1 activation.
source: Also, endocannabinoid release is triggered by mGluR1 activation, but the mGluR1 block did not affect the transient decrease of the PPR.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mGluR1 signaling.

claim: NO production has been linked to the activation of NMDARs in granule cell presynaptic boutons.
source: NO production has been linked to the activation of NMDARs in granule cell presynaptic boutons (Casado et al., 2002; Bidoret et al., 2009; Bidoret et al., 2015; Bouvier et al., 2016), or occasionally in molecular layer interneurons (Kono et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Casado et al., 2002; Bidoret et al., 2009; Bidoret et al., 2015; Bouvier et al., 2016.

claim: NO is a diffusible messenger and it activates the Guanylate Cyclase in the postsynaptic Purkinje cell.
source: NO is a diffusible messenger and it activates the Guanylate Cyclase in the postsynaptic Purkinje cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NO signaling.

claim: mGluR1s in Purkinje cells activate IP3-mediated Ca2+ release from stores.
source: They activate several downstream pathways, including IP3-mediated Ca2+ release from stores (Finch and Augustine, 1998; Takechi et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Finch and Augustine, 1998 and Takechi et al., 1998.

claim: mGluR1s in Purkinje cells mediate a slow EPSC mediating calcium entry.
source: a slow EPSC mediating calcium entry (Canepari et al., 2004; Canepari and Ogden, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Canepari et al., 2004 and Canepari and Ogden, 2006.

claim: mGluR1s regulate voltage-activated Ca2+ channels.
source: and regulate voltage-activated Ca2+ channels (Hildebrand et al., 2009; Otsu et al., 2014; Khawaled et al., 1999; Ait Ouares and Canepari, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hildebrand et al., 2009; Otsu et al., 2014; Khawaled et al., 1999; Ait Ouares and Canepari, 2020.

claim: The median PF-EPSC (288 pA, n=25) corresponds to approximately 34 active synapses.
source: The median PF-EPSC (288 pA, n=25) corresponds to approximately 34 active synapses (unitary amplitude for distal GC to PC connection is 8.4 pA Isope and Barbour, 2002).
evidence: This is calculated based on the median EPSC amplitude and unitary synaptic amplitude from Isope and Barbour, 2002.

claim: The median AA-EPSC (90 pA) would correspond to 11 active synapses and a total of 22 synapses.
source: For a similar unitary synaptic size, the median AA-EPSC (90 pA) would correspond to 11 active synapses and a total of 22 synapses (50% of local GC to PC connections are silent Isope and Barbour, 2002).
evidence: This is calculated based on the median EPSC amplitude and the proportion of silent synapses from Isope and Barbour, 2002.

claim: The recruited synapses represent less than 0.2% of the 175,000 excitatory synapses present on the dendritic tree of a PC.
source: These numbers represent less than 0.2% of the 175,000 excitatory synapses present on the dendritic tree of a PC (Napper and Harvey, 1988).
evidence: This is calculated based on the estimated number of recruited synapses and the total number of synapses from Napper and Harvey, 1988.

claim: mGluR1-mediated Ca2+ signals in Purkinje cells are not expected to propagate across the PC dendritic tree, because both Ca2+ and IP3 are quickly buffered.
source: mGluR1-mediated Ca2+ signals in Purkinje cells are not expected to propagate across the PC dendritic tree, because both Ca2+ and IP3 are quickly buffered.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Ca2+ and IP3 buffering in neurons.

claim: mGluR1-mediated Ca2+ release from stores is known to require priming by depolarisation.
source: On the other hand, mGluR1-mediated Ca2+ release from stores is known to require priming by depolarisation (Canepari and Ogden, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Canepari and Ogden, 2006.

claim: mGluR1 activation triggers the production of endocannabinoids.
source: mGluR1 activation also triggers the production of endocannabinoids (EC; Maejima et al., 2001; Brown et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maejima et al., 2001 and Brown et al., 2003.

claim: Presynaptic CB1Rs have been involved in PF-LTD.
source: and presynaptic CB1Rs have been involved in PF-LTD (Safo and Regehr, 2005; Carey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Safo and Regehr, 2005 and Carey et al., 2011.

claim: The induction protocol used, when applied to PF only and with inhibition preserved, was previously shown to induce PF-LTP.
source: This was unexpected because the induction protocol we used, when applied to PF only and with inhibition preserved, was previously shown to induce PF-LTP (Binda et al., 2016; Jörntell and Ekerot, 2002), although not always (González-Calvo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Binda et al., 2016 and Jörntell and Ekerot, 2002.

claim: PF-LTP was not sustained when inhibition was blocked during induction according to Binda et al., 2016.
source: But Binda et al., 2016 also showed that PF-LTP was not sustained when inhibition was blocked during induction, contradicting other studies performed with inhibition blocked (Bouvier et al., 2016; Piochon et al., 2016; Schonewille et al., 2021) with Picrotoxin or Bicuculline (a blocker of SK channels, Khawaled et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Binda et al., 2016.

claim: Hyperpolarisation by IPSCs relieves inactivation of T-type Ca2+ channels, themselves regulated by mGluR1, boosting Ca2+ signals and triggering PF-LTP.
source: Binda et al., 2016 showed that hyperpolarisation by IPSCs relieves inactivation of T-type Ca2+ channels, themselves regulated by mGluR1, boosting Ca2+ signals and triggering PF-LTP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Binda et al., 2016.

claim: Inhibition decreased Ca2+ entry, and as a result converted LTD into LTP according to Rowan et al., 2018.
source: On the other hand, the work by Rowan et al., 2018 indicated that inhibition decreased Ca2+ entry, and as a result converted LTD into LTP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rowan et al., 2018.

claim: AA synapses are suited to encode precise and selective information from the receptive field.
source: AA synapses are suited to encode precise and selective information from the receptive field, while PF synapses could efficiently represent context.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical considerations and the experimental findings.

claim: PF synapses could efficiently represent context.
source: AA synapses are suited to encode precise and selective information from the receptive field, while PF synapses could efficiently represent context.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical considerations and the experimental findings.

claim: The associative form of plasticity described is expected to reinforce AA signals presented conjointly with PF, or within a pertinent time window, while attenuating signals presented in isolation.
source: The associative form of plasticity we describe, together with the time dependence, is expected to reinforce AA signals presented conjointly with PF, or within a pertinent time window, while attenuating signals presented in isolation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings about associative plasticity and timing dependence.

claim: Associative plasticity in PCs can be triggered by granule cell inputs independently of the climbing fibre.
source: This work shows that associative plasticity in PCs can be triggered by granule cell inputs independently of the climbing fibre, requiring only moderate inputs, in contrast with the powerful CF, which triggers widespread depolarisation and Ca2+ increase.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings showing AA-LTP without CF stimulation.

claim: The climbing fibre is classically associated with error signals and learning.
source: The climbing fibre is classically associated with error signals and learning (Aiba et al., 1994; Ito and Kano, 1982; Marr, 1969; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Aiba et al., 1994; Ito and Kano, 1982; Marr, 1969; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2014.

claim: Both climbing fibre and granule cells have been shown to encode reward signals.
source: However, both climbing fibre (Kostadinov et al., 2019) and granule cells Wagner et al., 2017 have been shown to encode reward signals, which might be important in driving plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kostadinov et al., 2019 and Wagner et al., 2017.

claim: Experiments were performed on horizontal slices 300 µm thick cut from the cerebellum of 19–25-day-old Sprague-Dawley male or female rats.
source: Experiments were performed on horizontal slices 300 µm thick cut from the cerebellum of 19–25- day-old Sprague-Dawley male or female rats.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental preparation.

claim: At this age, GC synapses are well-established.
source: At this age, GC synapses are well-established (Ichikawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ichikawa et al., 2016.

claim: The low Cl- concentration in the intracellular solution ensured the reversal potential for Cl- was close to the value determined for PCs (–85 mV).
source: The low Cl- concentration in the intracellular solution ensured the reversal potential for Cl- was close to the value determined for PCs (–85 mV, Chavas and Marty, 2003)
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citation to Chavas and Marty, 2003.
